notes.description: A single layer of flattened epithelial cells specialized for rapid diffusion and filtration.
notes.location: Alveoli of lungs, endothelium of blood vessels, Bowman's capsule of kidney.
notes.function: Allows exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products through thin barriers.
notes.features: Very thin cells with flattened nuclei. Cells appear like a mosaic when viewed from the surface.
notes.clinical: Damage to alveolar simple squamous epithelium can impair gas exchange in lung diseases.

notes.description: A single layer of cube-shaped epithelial cells involved in secretion and absorption.
notes.location: Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, small gland ducts.
notes.features: Round central nuclei with cells approximately equal in height and width.
notes.clinical: Changes in renal tubular epithelium may occur during kidney injury.

notes.description: A specialized epithelium capable of stretching and changing shape.
notes.function: Allows expansion of urinary organs while maintaining a protective barrier.
notes.features: Multiple layers of cells with rounded superficial umbrella cells.
notes.clinical: Abnormal transitional epithelial changes may be associated with urinary tract tumors.

notes.description: Liver tissue organized into hepatic lobules containing hepatocytes and sinusoids.
notes.location: Largest internal organ located in the right upper abdomen.
notes.function: Metabolism, detoxification, bile production, and plasma protein synthesis.
notes.features: Central vein surrounded by plates of hepatocytes with blood sinusoids.
notes.clinical: Chronic injury can lead to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

notes.description: Renal tissue containing nephrons responsible for filtration and urine formation.
notes.location: Retroperitoneal organs on either side of the vertebral column.
notes.function: Blood filtration, electrolyte regulation, and hormone production.
notes.features: Glomeruli, proximal tubules, distal tubules, and collecting ducts.
notes.clinical: Histological changes help identify kidney diseases such as glomerulonephritis.

notes.description: Mineralized connective tissue providing structural support and protection.
notes.function: Support, protection, mineral storage, and blood cell formation.
notes.features: Osteons containing central canals surrounded by concentric lamellae.
notes.clinical: Bone remodeling disorders can affect strength and fracture risk.

notes.description:
A – Lumen

Central space through which blood flows.

B – Tunica Intima

Thin inner layer lined by simple squamous endothelium and supported by subendothelial connective tissue.

C – Internal Elastic Lamina

Prominent wavy elastic membrane separating the tunica intima from the tunica media. It is often one of the easiest features to identify.

D – Tunica Media

Thick layer composed predominantly of circularly arranged smooth muscle cells. This is the most prominent layer in muscular arteries.

E – External Elastic Lamina

Elastic membrane separating the tunica media from the tunica adventitia. It may be distinct or less conspicuous depending on the specimen.

F – Tunica Adventitia (Tunica Externa)

Outer connective tissue layer containing collagen fibers, elastic fibers, fibroblasts, nerves, and occasionally small blood vessels (vasa vasorum in larger arteries).

Description

Muscular arteries are medium-sized distributing arteries that transport blood from elastic arteries to specific organs and tissues. Their thick smooth muscle layer allows regulation of blood flow and blood pressure through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
notes.location:
Examples include:

Radial artery
Femoral artery
Brachial artery
Ulnar artery
Coronary arteries
Mesenteric arteries
notes.function:
Distribute blood to organs and tissues.
Regulate blood pressure through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
Control regional blood flow according to tissue demands.
notes.features:
Identifying Features
Thick tunica media composed mainly of smooth muscle.
Distinct, wavy internal elastic lamina.
Round or oval lumen that generally maintains its shape.
Tunica media thicker than the tunica adventitia.
Endothelium lining the lumen.
External elastic lamina may be visible.
notes.clinical: Muscular arteries are commonly affected by atherosclerosis, where lipid-rich plaques develop within the tunica intima, narrowing the lumen and reducing blood flow. Persistent hypertension can also lead to thickening of the arterial wall, increasing vascular resistance and contributing to cardiovascular disease.

notes.description:
Tags

A – Lumen

Central passage through which food and liquids travel.

B – Non-keratinized Stratified Squamous Epithelium

Thick protective lining that resists abrasion during swallowing.

C – Lamina Propria

Loose connective tissue immediately beneath the epithelium containing blood vessels, immune cells, and occasional esophageal glands near the ends of the organ.

D – Muscularis Mucosae

Thin layer of longitudinal smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the submucosa.

E – Submucosa

Dense irregular connective tissue containing larger blood vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and esophageal glands proper.

F – Esophageal Glands

Mucous glands located in the submucosa that secrete mucus to lubricate the lumen.

G – Muscularis Externa

Two muscle layers responsible for peristalsis:

Inner circular layer
Outer longitudinal layer

H – Adventitia (or Serosa if abdominal portion)

Outer connective tissue layer anchoring the esophagus to surrounding structures. Only the short abdominal segment is covered by serosa.

Description

The esophagus is a muscular tube that transports food from the pharynx to the stomach. Histologically, it is characterized by a thick non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium for protection against abrasion and a submucosa containing mucous glands that lubricate the passage of food.
notes.location: Extends from the pharynx, through the neck and thorax, passes through the diaphragm, and joins the stomach at the gastroesophageal junction.
notes.function:
Conducts food and liquids from the pharynx to the stomach.
Lubricates the food bolus through mucus secretion.
Protects underlying tissues from mechanical abrasion.
Propels food by coordinated peristaltic contractions.
notes.features:
Thick non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Prominent muscularis mucosae.
Submucosal mucous glands.
Muscularis externa with inner circular and outer longitudinal layers.
Muscle composition changes along its length:
Upper third: skeletal muscle
Middle third: mixed skeletal and smooth muscle
Lower third: smooth muscle
Absence of villi and gastric pits.
notes.clinical: The esophagus is commonly affected by gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), where chronic acid exposure damages the squamous epithelium. Persistent reflux may lead to Barrett's esophagus, in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium, increasing the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

notes.description:
Tags

A – Lumen

Central air passage through which air flows.

B – Mucosa

Inner lining consisting of the respiratory epithelium and underlying connective tissue.

C – Submucosa

Connective tissue layer containing blood vessels, nerves, and seromucous glands.

D – Hyaline Cartilage

C-shaped cartilage ring that supports the tracheal wall and prevents airway collapse.

E – Trachealis Muscle

Smooth muscle located on the posterior aspect of the trachea, connecting the ends of the cartilage ring.

F – Adventitia

Outer connective tissue layer that anchors the trachea to surrounding structures.

Description

The trachea is a conducting airway lined by respiratory epithelium and supported by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. Its mucosa contains ciliated cells and goblet cells that form the mucociliary escalator, while submucosal seromucous glands help humidify inspired air.
notes.location: Extends from the larynx (approximately C6 vertebral level) to the carina, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi (approximately T4–T5).
notes.function:
Conducts air between the larynx and bronchi.
Filters inhaled particles through mucus.
Moves mucus and debris toward the pharynx via ciliary action.
Humidifies and warms inspired air.
Prevents airway collapse through hyaline cartilage support.
notes.features:
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
Numerous goblet cells.
Thick basement membrane.
Seromucous glands in the submucosa.
Prominent C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings.
Trachealis smooth muscle on the posterior aspect.
No alveoli present.
notes.clinical: Damage to the cilia from cigarette smoking impairs mucociliary clearance, increasing the risk of respiratory infections and chronic bronchitis. In tracheomalacia, weakening of the tracheal cartilage leads to airway collapse during breathing.

notes.description:
A – Lumen

Large central cavity that commonly contains numerous spermatozoa.

B – Pseudostratified Columnar Epithelium

Tall epithelial lining with stereocilia, responsible for sperm maturation and absorption of excess fluid.

The epididymis is a long, highly coiled duct that receives sperm from the testis. Histologically, it is composed of numerous circular or oval duct profiles lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia. The lumen often contains abundant spermatozoa, and the surrounding smooth muscle facilitates sperm transport.
notes.location: Situated along the posterior surface of each testis and continuous with the vas deferens.
notes.function:
Maturation of spermatozoa.
Storage of sperm prior to ejaculation.
Reabsorption of excess testicular fluid.
Transport of sperm to the vas deferens by smooth muscle contraction.
notes.features:
Numerous closely packed, coiled ducts.
Large lumina, often filled with spermatozoa.
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.
Smooth muscle surrounding each duct.
Thin connective tissue between adjacent ducts.
notes.clinical: Inflammation of the epididymis (epididymitis) is commonly caused by bacterial infections, including sexually transmitted pathogens in younger men and urinary tract organisms in older men. Chronic inflammation may impair sperm transport and contribute to male infertility.

notes.description:
A – Lumen

Central cavity containing numerous spermatozoa.

B – Spermatozoa

Mature sperm cells seen within the lumen as densely packed, thread-like material.

C – Pseudostratified Columnar Epithelium

Epithelial lining composed mainly of principal and basal cells.

D – Stereocilia

Long, non-motile apical projections extending into the lumen that increase the absorptive surface area.

E – Principal Cells

Tall columnar cells responsible for absorption of testicular fluid and secretion of factors that promote sperm maturation.

F – Basal Cells

Small, round cells located near the basement membrane that serve as stem cells for epithelial renewal.

G – Basement Membrane

Thin supporting layer separating the epithelium from the underlying connective tissue.

H – Smooth Muscle

Circular layer of smooth muscle surrounding the duct, responsible for propelling sperm during ejaculation.

Description

The epididymis is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia and contains abundant spermatozoa within its lumen. At higher magnification, the principal cells, basal cells, and stereocilia become readily distinguishable. The surrounding smooth muscle assists in sperm transport.
notes.location: Located along the posterior border of the testis and continuous with the ductus (vas) deferens.
notes.function:
Maturation of spermatozoa.
Storage of mature sperm.
Reabsorption of excess luminal fluid.
Propulsion of sperm into the vas deferens during ejaculation.
notes.features:
Wide lumen packed with spermatozoa.
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
Long stereocilia on principal cells.
Basal cells adjacent to the basement membrane.
Thin smooth muscle surrounding each duct.
notes.clinical: Obstruction or inflammation of the epididymis (epididymitis) can interfere with sperm maturation and transport, potentially leading to reduced fertility. Histologically, chronic inflammation may show epithelial damage and infiltration by inflammatory cells.

notes.description:
A – Enamel

Highly mineralized outer covering of the crown. In decalcified sections, it may appear as a clear space or may be absent due to removal during processing.

B – Dentin

Thick calcified tissue beneath the enamel forming the bulk of the tooth.

C – Pulp Cavity

Central chamber containing loose connective tissue, blood vessels, nerves, and odontoblasts.

D – Odontoblast Layer

Single layer of tall cells lining the periphery of the pulp cavity responsible for dentin formation.

E – Cementum

Thin calcified layer covering the root of the tooth.

F – Periodontal Ligament

Dense connective tissue attaching the cementum to the alveolar bone.

G – Alveolar Bone

Bone surrounding the tooth socket that anchors the tooth within the jaw.

The tooth is a calcified structure specialized for mastication. At low magnification, the major tissues of the tooth—including enamel, dentin, pulp cavity, cementum, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone—can be identified. Dentin forms the largest portion of the tooth, while the pulp occupies the central cavity and contains its neurovascular supply.
notes.location: Embedded within the alveolar sockets of the maxilla and mandible.
notes.function:
Mastication (chewing food).
Protection of the dental pulp.
Transmission of sensory stimuli.
Support of occlusion during biting and chewing.
notes.features:
Thick dentin forming the bulk of the tooth.
Central pulp cavity.
Outer enamel covering the crown (may appear absent in decalcified sections).
Cementum covering the root.
Periodontal ligament between cementum and alveolar bone.
Surrounding alveolar bone.
notes.clinical: Dental caries begin with demineralization of the enamel and may progress into the dentin and pulp, causing pulpitis and severe tooth pain. Periodontal disease affects the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, potentially resulting in tooth mobility and tooth loss.

notes.description:
A – Urethra (Penile/Spongy Urethra)

Central passage within the corpus spongiosum that conveys urine and semen.

B – Corpus Spongiosum

Erectile tissue surrounding the urethra that prevents urethral compression during erection.

C – Corpus Cavernosum

Large paired erectile bodies composed of vascular spaces responsible for penile rigidity during erection.

D – Trabeculae

Connective tissue and smooth muscle partitions separating the vascular spaces within the erectile tissue.

E – Cavernous (Vascular) Spaces

Large blood-filled sinusoids that engorge with blood during erection.

F – Tunica Albuginea

Dense fibrous connective tissue capsule surrounding each corpus cavernosum.

G – Deep Artery of the Penis

Artery located within each corpus cavernosum supplying blood to the erectile tissue.

Description

The penis is composed of three cylindrical masses of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa dorsally and one corpus spongiosum ventrally enclosing the penile urethra. At low magnification, the erectile tissues are characterized by numerous vascular spaces separated by connective tissue trabeculae and enclosed by the tunica albuginea.
notes.location: External male genital organ, extending from the pubic region to the external urethral orifice.
notes.function:
Delivers semen during ejaculation.
Conducts urine from the bladder to the exterior.
Achieves erection through engorgement of erectile tissue with blood.
notes.features:
Two large corpora cavernosa.
One corpus spongiosum surrounding the urethra.
Numerous vascular (cavernous) spaces.
Thick tunica albuginea around the corpora cavernosa.
Connective tissue trabeculae separating the vascular spaces.
Deep artery within each corpus cavernosum.
notes.clinical: Erectile dysfunction may result from impaired arterial blood flow, nerve injury, or damage to the erectile tissue. In Peyronie's disease, fibrosis of the tunica albuginea causes abnormal penile curvature and may interfere with normal erection.

notes.description:
A – Anterior Pituitary (Pars Distalis)

Darkly stained, highly cellular region containing hormone-secreting endocrine cells.

B – Posterior Pituitary (Pars Nervosa)

Lightly stained region composed mainly of unmyelinated nerve fibers and supporting glial cells (pituicytes).

C – Pars Intermedia

Thin zone between the anterior and posterior pituitary, often containing small colloid-filled cysts (Rathke's cysts).

D – Connective Tissue Capsule

Thin fibrous capsule surrounding the gland.

E – Blood Sinusoids

Wide fenestrated capillaries interspersed among the endocrine cells, facilitating hormone release into the bloodstream.

Description

The pituitary gland is the master endocrine gland, consisting of an anterior glandular lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior neural lobe (neurohypophysis). At low magnification, the anterior pituitary appears darker due to its densely packed endocrine cells, while the posterior pituitary is lighter because it is composed mainly of nerve fibers and supporting cells.
notes.location: Situated within the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, attached to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum.
notes.function:
Secretes hormones regulating growth, metabolism, reproduction, lactation, and stress responses.
Stores and releases oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) produced by the hypothalamus.
notes.features:
Distinct dark-staining anterior pituitary (pars distalis).
Pale-staining posterior pituitary (pars nervosa).
Pars intermedia located between the two lobes.
Numerous blood sinusoids within the anterior pituitary.
Thin connective tissue capsule surrounding the gland.
notes.clinical: Pituitary adenomas are the most common tumors of the pituitary gland and may cause excessive hormone secretion (such as prolactin or growth hormone) or compress surrounding structures, leading to headaches and visual disturbances, particularly bitemporal hemianopia due to optic chiasm compression.

notes.description: test

The adrenal cortex is the outer portion of the adrenal (suprarenal) gland. It is composed of steroid-secreting endocrine cells arranged in three concentric zones:

Zona glomerulosa – outermost
Zona fasciculata – middle and largest
Zona reticularis – innermost

The cells have abundant lipid droplets, giving the cortex a characteristic pale/foamy appearance, especially in the zona fasciculata.
notes.location:
Forms the outer ~80–90% of the adrenal gland.
Lies immediately beneath the fibrous connective tissue capsule.
Surrounds the adrenal medulla, which forms the central region.
Adrenal glands are located superior to the kidneys in the retroperitoneum.
notes.function:
The adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones:

Zone	Main hormone(s)	Main function
Zona glomerulosa	Aldosterone	Na+ retention, K+ excretion, regulation of blood pressure
Zona fasciculata	Cortisol	Stress response, increased blood glucose, metabolic regulation, anti-inflammatory effects
Zona reticularis	Androgens (DHEA, androstenedione)	Contribute to secondary sexual characteristics and libido

Mnemonic: GFR → Salt, Sugar, Sex

Glomerulosa → Salt → aldosterone
Fasciculata → Sugar → cortisol
Reticularis → Sex → androgens
notes.features:
Three distinct cortical zones can be identified.
Zona glomerulosa: small cells arranged in rounded clusters/arches.
Zona fasciculata: large, pale, foamy cells arranged in straight cords extending toward the medulla; usually the widest zone.
Zona reticularis: smaller, darker-staining cells arranged in an irregular network (anastomosing cords).
Cells contain abundant lipid droplets because steroid hormones are synthesized from cholesterol.
Rich sinusoidal capillary network between cellular cords.
Cortex is separated from the medulla by the corticomedullary junction.
notes.clinical:
Cushing syndrome: excess cortisol → central obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, muscle wasting, and characteristic skin changes.
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome): excess aldosterone → hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.
Addison disease: adrenal cortical insufficiency → low cortisol and aldosterone, hypotension, weakness and electrolyte abnormalities; primary disease may cause hyperpigmentation due to increased ACTH.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: inherited defects in steroid synthesis, commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency, causing impaired cortisol synthesis with increased adrenal androgen production.
Adrenocortical tumors may produce excess cortisol, aldosterone or androgens depending on the zone involved.
